topics.name: An Inspector Calls (Component 01, Section A)
subtopics: No extract is printed for the modern text question - you write a whole-play essay from a choice of two questions
J. B. Priestley's socialist purpose: writing in 1945 about events set in 1912, warning post-war Britain against returning to pre-war selfishness
Mr Birling: capitalist complacency, dramatic irony over the Titanic and 'the war will never happen'
Mrs Birling: hypocrisy, class snobbery, denial of responsibility towards Eva Smith
Sheila: the character who changes most, from spoilt fiancee to someone who accepts collective responsibility
Eric: drinking, financial dependence, theft, and his own culpability with Eva
Gerald Croft: the 'man of the world', his affair with Daisy Renton, and his relief when the Inspector is exposed as possibly false
Inspector Goole: mouthpiece for Priestley, omniscient control of pace and revelations, symbolic surname (ghoul)
Eva Smith/Daisy Renton: never appears on stage, represents the exploited working class and the invisibility of the poor
The cyclical structure: the final telephone call repeats the Act One announcement, trapping the family in the same crisis
Dramatic irony throughout, built from the audience's 1945 knowledge of two world wars and the Titanic's sinking
Stagecraft: the single set, the lighting change from 'pink and intimate' to 'brighter and harder', the doorbell as a structural device
Themes: collective versus individual responsibility, class and privilege, capitalism versus socialism, generational divide (older Birlings versus Sheila and Eric)
The play as a moral fable or 'well-made play' with a three-act structure building to a twist
Context: the 1912 setting (pre-Titanic, pre-war optimism) versus the 1945 audience who had lived through the Second World War and the founding of the welfare state
Key scenes: the engagement toast in Act One, the Inspector's exit speech ('fire and blood and anguish'), the final telephone call

cards.front: Why did Priestley set An Inspector Calls in 1912 but write it in 1945?
cards.back: To use dramatic irony: the 1945 audience knew the 1912 optimism about peace and prosperity (and the Titanic) was about to be shattered, reinforcing his warning against complacency.

cards.front: How does Sheila change across the play?
cards.back: She moves from a spoilt, jealous fiancee in Act One to the character who most fully accepts responsibility and challenges her parents' refusal to learn, showing Priestley's hope for the younger generation.

cards.front: What is the dramatic function of the Inspector's exit speech?
cards.back: It delivers Priestley's central socialist message directly to the audience: that if people do not learn collective responsibility, the world faces 'fire and blood and anguish' - a warning about war.

cards.front: Why does Priestley never let Eva Smith appear on stage?
cards.back: It keeps the focus on how each character treats her, turning her into a symbol of the invisible, exploited working class rather than an individual the audience can dismiss.

cards.front: What is significant about the play's final telephone call?
cards.back: It repeats the opening announcement almost exactly, creating a cyclical structure that suggests the family's chance to learn may be about to repeat, or that they cannot escape the consequences of their actions.

cards.front: How does Mr Birling's dramatic irony work in Act One?
cards.back: His confident, factually wrong predictions (Titanic 'unsinkable', no war coming) immediately undermine his authority for the audience, discrediting his capitalist worldview from the start.

cards.front: What does Gerald's reaction to the Inspector possibly being fake reveal?
cards.back: His relief shows he wants to escape moral responsibility rather than learn from what happened, aligning him with the older generation despite his youth.

cards.front: What does the surname 'Goole' suggest about the Inspector?
cards.back: It sounds like 'ghoul', hinting he may be supernatural, a moral force, or Eva's avenging conscience rather than a literal police inspector.

cards.front: Give two ways stagecraft controls mood in the play.
cards.back: The single continuous set keeps tension concentrated in one room, and the lighting shifts from 'pink and intimate' to 'brighter and harder' when the Inspector arrives, exposing the family.

cards.front: What is the central thematic conflict of the play?
cards.back: Individual responsibility and capitalism (the Birlings' view) versus collective responsibility and socialism (the Inspector's view), reflecting Priestley's own political beliefs.

cloze: An Inspector Calls is set in {{c1::1912}} but was written and first performed in {{c2::1945}}.
The Inspector's surname, {{c1::Goole}}, hints that he may be a {{c2::supernatural}} or moral force rather than a real policeman.
{{c1::Sheila}} is the character who changes most across the play, ending by challenging her parents.
The play ends with a {{c1::telephone call}} that repeats the opening announcement, creating a {{c2::cyclical}} structure.
Priestley uses the 1912 setting for {{c1::dramatic irony}}, since the audience knew the Titanic would sink and war would follow.

topics.name: The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (Component 01, Section B)
subtopics: A printed extract question: analyse the given extract, then range across the whole novel
Robert Louis Stevenson writing in 1886 for a late-Victorian audience anxious about science, morality and respectability
Structure: a framed, multi-narrator novel - Utterson's third-person narrative, then Lanyon's letter, then Jekyll's final confession
The withholding of information: the mystery-thriller structure delays the reveal that Jekyll and Hyde are one person
Duality as the central idea: every man is 'not truly one, but truly two', a battle between civilised self and primitive urges
Dr Jekyll: respectable, repressed, scientifically curious, ultimately consumed by his own experiment
Mr Hyde: physically smaller, described as ape-like, primitive, associated with violence (Carew murder) and instinctive evil
Mr Utterson: the reliable, restrained lawyer whose investigation structures the reader's discovery of the truth
Dr Lanyon: the rational scientist destroyed by witnessing something that defies his scientific worldview
Victorian context: strict codes of respectability and reputation, fear of being publicly disgraced
Context: the Victorian double life, hidden vice behind a respectable public facade (echoes of real cases and Darwinian anxiety about man's animal nature)
Context: contemporary science, evolutionary theory, and fears that science could unleash uncontrollable forces
Gothic conventions: fog-bound London streets, locked doors, a sinister house, the uncanny, transformation/transgression
Symbolism: the door as a barrier between public and private selves, the two entrances to Jekyll's house
Key scenes: Enfield's account of Hyde trampling the girl, the Carew murder, Lanyon's witnessing of the transformation, Jekyll's final statement
Jekyll's final confession as a first-person unravelling of motive, guilt and loss of control over the transformations

cards.front: What is the central duality explored in Jekyll and Hyde?
cards.back: Stevenson presents every person as containing both a civilised, respectable self and a primitive, immoral self - 'man is not truly one, but truly two'.

cards.front: Why does Stevenson delay revealing that Jekyll and Hyde are the same person?
cards.back: The novel is structured as a mystery; withholding the connection builds suspense and lets the reader experience Utterson's own confusion and investigation.

cards.front: What is the effect of using multiple narrators (Utterson, Lanyon's letter, Jekyll's confession)?
cards.back: Each narrator has a different degree of knowledge and reliability, gradually revealing more of the truth and letting Stevenson delay full disclosure until the very end.

cards.front: How is Hyde physically described, and why?
cards.back: As smaller, ape-like and giving an instinctive impression of deformity - his appearance reflects an atavistic, animalistic morality, tying into Victorian anxiety about evolution.

cards.front: Why does Dr Lanyon die after witnessing the transformation?
cards.back: As a rational man of science, witnessing Hyde transform into Jekyll shatters his entire scientific worldview - the shock destroys him.

cards.front: What does the locked door and Jekyll's cabinet symbolise?
cards.back: The barrier between Jekyll's respectable public life and his hidden, secret self - a physical symbol of Victorian double lives.

cards.front: How does the novel reflect Victorian anxieties about respectability?
cards.back: Jekyll's fear of public disgrace drives him to create Hyde as an outlet for desires he cannot express respectably, mirroring real Victorian fears of hidden vice behind a public facade.

cards.front: What role does fog play in the novel's setting?
cards.back: It is a Gothic device that obscures and disorientates, mirroring the moral confusion and hidden truths at the heart of the story, and reflects real Victorian London smog.

cards.front: How does Jekyll lose control over his transformations?
cards.back: What begins as a deliberate, controlled experiment becomes involuntary - Hyde starts to emerge without the potion, showing addiction and the danger of indulging one's darker nature.

cards.front: What is significant about Jekyll's final written confession?
cards.back: It is the only first-person account in the novel, finally giving the reader Jekyll's own motives, guilt and admission that he created Hyde to escape moral responsibility for his vices.

cloze: Stevenson presents every person as containing two natures: man is 'not truly {{c1::one}}, but truly {{c2::two}}'.
The novel withholds the truth that {{c1::Jekyll}} and {{c2::Hyde}} are the same person until near the end.
{{c1::Dr Lanyon}} dies after witnessing the transformation because it destroys his rational, scientific worldview.
Hyde is described as {{c1::ape-like}}, reflecting Victorian anxiety about {{c2::evolution}} and man's animal nature.
The final chapter is {{c1::Jekyll's}} own written confession, told in the first person.

topics.name: Macbeth (Component 02, Section B)
subtopics: A printed extract question: analyse the given extract, then discuss the whole play
Shakespeare writing around 1606 for James I, who believed in the divine right of kings and had survived the Gunpowder Plot
The three witches (Weird Sisters): ambiguous prophecy, supernatural temptation, and Jacobean beliefs about witchcraft
Macbeth's initial nobility (Sergeant's report, 'brave Macbeth') set against his rapid moral decline
Macbeth's soliloquies as windows into a conscience at war with ambition ('If it were done, when 'tis done'; 'dagger' soliloquy)
Lady Macbeth: ambition, manipulation of Macbeth's masculinity, the sleepwalking and hand-washing that reveal guilt she cannot voice
The motif of blood: from 'brave Macbeth' with 'smoking' blade to Lady Macbeth's inability to wash imagined blood from her hands
The motif of darkness and unnatural disorder: disrupted sleep, storms, and the natural world reacting to regicide
Banquo: Macbeth's foil, murdered out of paranoia, whose ghost appears at the banquet as a symbol of guilt
Macduff: the avenging hero, learns of his family's murder, kills Macbeth in the final act, restoring order
Duncan: the rightful, divinely-sanctioned king, whose murder is a crime against both the state and natural/divine order
The theme of ambition and its corrupting effect on both Macbeths
The theme of kingship: contrast between Duncan's/Malcolm's legitimate rule and Macbeth's tyranny
The theme of the supernatural and fate versus free will - do the witches control Macbeth or merely reveal his own desires
Key scenes: the witches' first prophecy (Act 1), Duncan's murder (Act 2), Banquo's ghost at the banquet (Act 3), the sleepwalking scene (Act 5), the final duel with Macduff
Dramatic irony and structure: the rise-and-fall tragic arc typical of Shakespearean tragedy, with the order of Scotland restored under Malcolm at the end

cards.front: Why might Shakespeare have written Macbeth to flatter King James I?
cards.back: James I believed in the divine right of kings and claimed descent from Banquo; the play condemns regicide and shows witchcraft (a subject James wrote about) as a real, dangerous force.

cards.front: How does Macbeth change from Act 1 to Act 5?
cards.back: He moves from a brave, loyal general praised by the Sergeant to a paranoid tyrant who murders friends and children, showing the corrupting effect of unchecked ambition.

cards.front: What is the dramatic function of Macbeth's soliloquies?
cards.back: They reveal his internal conflict between ambition and conscience, letting the audience see the moral cost of his actions that other characters cannot.

cards.front: How does Lady Macbeth manipulate Macbeth before Duncan's murder?
cards.back: She questions his masculinity and courage, telling him to 'screw your courage to the sticking-place', pushing him past his own doubts.

cards.front: Trace the blood motif across the play.
cards.back: Macbeth is first praised for his bloody, heroic actions in battle; after Duncan's murder blood becomes a symbol of guilt, culminating in Lady Macbeth's hallucinated bloodstains she cannot wash away.

cards.front: What does Banquo's ghost at the banquet represent?
cards.back: Macbeth's guilty conscience made visible - only he can see the ghost, showing his growing psychological disintegration and isolation.

cards.front: How does Shakespeare use the natural world to reflect the murder of Duncan?
cards.back: Unnatural disorder follows the regicide - storms, strange animal behaviour and darkness during daytime - reflecting the Jacobean belief that killing a king disrupted the natural and divine order.

cards.front: What is Macduff's dramatic role in the play?
cards.back: He is the avenging hero who loses his family to Macbeth's tyranny and ultimately kills Macbeth, restoring rightful order under Malcolm.

cards.front: Do the witches control Macbeth's fate, or reveal his own ambition?
cards.back: This is deliberately ambiguous - the prophecy could be read as manipulating him, or simply voicing an ambition that was already within him, which he then chooses to act on.

cards.front: What does the sleepwalking scene reveal about Lady Macbeth?
cards.back: Unlike her earlier confident ruthlessness, she is now consumed by guilt she cannot control or voice while awake, showing psychological collapse.

cloze: Macbeth is first described by the Sergeant as {{c1::brave}} before his moral decline begins.
Lady Macbeth tells Macbeth to 'screw your {{c1::courage}} to the sticking-place' to push him towards murder.
{{c1::Banquo's ghost}} appears at the banquet, visible only to Macbeth, symbolising his guilt.
After Duncan's murder, {{c1::blood}} becomes a recurring symbol of guilt that cannot be washed away.
{{c1::Macduff}} kills Macbeth in the final act, restoring order under {{c2::Malcolm}}.

topics.name: OCR Poetry Anthology: Love and Relationships Cluster
subtopics: This cluster is one of three options in the OCR Poetry Anthology 'Towards a World Unknown' - the family has not confirmed which cluster is studied, so treat this as preparation only until confirmed
The exam gives one named poem printed on the paper, plus a linked unseen poem; you compare the named poem with the unseen poem and may also be asked about a second anthology poem
Do not guess specific poem titles you are not certain belong to this cluster - focus revision on themes, comparative method and named poems only where certain
Likely thematic range for a Love and Relationships cluster: romantic love, loss of love, family bonds, one-sided or unrequited love, love across distance or time, the pain and joy love can bring
Comparative method: identify a shared theme or attitude between the named poem and the unseen poem, then compare how each poet presents it

Poetic form and structure relevant to love poetry: the sonnet form and its traditional association with romantic love, dramatic monologue giving one voice's perspective, structure that shifts at a volta
Voice and perspective: whether a poem is spoken in first person, addressed directly to a lover, or narrated about a relationship from outside
Imagery patterns common in love poetry: nature imagery for growth or decay of feeling, domestic imagery for intimacy, extended metaphor for a relationship
Tone shifts within a single poem, e.g. from tenderness to anger, or nostalgia to acceptance
Sound and rhythm: how rhyme scheme, metre or its absence (free verse) can mirror harmony or discord in a relationship
Comparing methods, not just content: two poems can share a theme (loss) but use very different techniques to convey it
Building flexible comparison points: form, structure, imagery, tone and language choices that can be adapted to whichever named poem appears
Practising with any unseen love-themed poem to build confidence comparing methods under time pressure
Revision priority: since the studied poems are unconfirmed, prioritise comparative skills and terminology over memorising specific poem content

cards.front: How is the Poetry Anthology question on Component 02 structured?
cards.back: One named poem from your studied cluster is printed on the paper alongside a linked unseen poem; you compare how both poems present a given theme, focusing on methods.

cards.front: Why does this revision set avoid naming specific poems in the Love and Relationships cluster?
cards.back: The family has not confirmed which OCR poetry cluster is studied, and the specific poem list has not been independently verified, so guessing titles risks embedding wrong facts - only certain themes and methods are covered.

cards.front: What comparative approach should you use regardless of which poems appear?
cards.back: Identify a shared idea or theme first, then compare each poet's methods (form, structure, imagery, tone) for presenting it, rather than describing each poem separately.

cards.front: Why is the sonnet form often associated with love poetry?
cards.back: Its traditional 14-line structure and volta (turn) suit exploring a single idea about love and then complicating or resolving it, a pattern many love poems adapt or subvert.

cards.front: What is a dramatic monologue and why might it suit a love poem?
cards.back: A poem spoken in a single created voice, which can reveal a speaker's feelings about a relationship more intimately, including feelings they may not fully realise themselves.

cards.front: Give an example of how imagery might mirror a relationship in a love poem.
cards.back: Nature imagery (blossoming, withering) can mirror the growth or decline of feeling, while domestic imagery can convey intimacy or entrapment within a relationship.

cards.front: How can rhyme and rhythm reflect the state of a relationship?
cards.back: A regular, harmonious rhyme scheme can suggest a stable or contented relationship, while broken rhythm, irregular line lengths or free verse can suggest conflict or emotional turmoil.

cards.front: What is the risk of comparing two poems 'poem by poem'?
cards.back: It tends to become description of each poem in turn rather than sustained comparison, which limits marks for comparative analysis of methods.

cloze: The Love and Relationships cluster is one of {{c1::three}} themed clusters in the OCR Poetry Anthology.
In the exam, a {{c1::named}} poem is printed alongside a linked {{c2::unseen}} poem for comparison.
A poem spoken in a single created voice is called a {{c1::dramatic monologue}}.
A {{c1::volta}} is a turn or shift in a poem's argument or mood, often used in sonnets about love.

topics.name: OCR Poetry Anthology: Conflict Cluster
subtopics: This cluster is one of three options in the OCR Poetry Anthology 'Towards a World Unknown' - the family has not confirmed which cluster is studied, so treat this as preparation only until confirmed
The exam gives one named poem printed on the paper, plus a linked unseen poem; you compare the named poem with the unseen poem and may also be asked about a second anthology poem
Do not guess specific poem titles you are not certain belong to this cluster - focus revision on themes, comparative method and named poems only where certain

Likely thematic range for a Conflict cluster: physical war and battle, the psychological aftermath of conflict, conflict between generations or cultures, inner emotional conflict, the cost of conflict to ordinary people
Perspective in conflict poetry: soldier's first-hand voice, a civilian or bystander's view, or a distanced/reflective narrator looking back
Imagery patterns common in conflict poetry: violent or visceral physical imagery, imagery of destruction and ruin, contrasting imagery of peace or home to heighten the horror of conflict
Structural devices: fragmented or disrupted structure to mirror chaos, regular structure used ironically to suggest false order, enjambment to create urgency or breathlessness
Tone in conflict poetry: anger, grief, irony, numbness, or a controlled, restrained tone that lets horror speak for itself
Sound devices: harsh consonants and plosives for violence, caesura for sudden shock or interruption
Comparative method: identify a shared idea about conflict (its cost, its glorification, its aftermath) then compare how each poet's methods present it differently
Comparing attitudes to conflict: some poems may glorify or question, condemn or memorialise - identify the poet's stance as part of the comparison
Building flexible comparison points around structure, imagery, tone and form so they can be adapted to whichever named poem appears
Practising with any unseen conflict-themed poem to build confidence comparing methods under time pressure
Revision priority: since the studied poems are unconfirmed, prioritise comparative skills and terminology over memorising specific poem content

cards.front: What kinds of conflict might appear across poems in this cluster?
cards.back: Physical war and battle, the psychological aftermath of conflict for soldiers or civilians, conflict between generations or cultures, and inner emotional conflict.

cards.front: Why might a poet use fragmented or disrupted structure in a conflict poem?
cards.back: To mirror the chaos, disorientation or trauma of conflict, rather than presenting events in a calm, orderly way.

cards.front: How can caesura be used effectively in a conflict poem?
cards.back: A sudden pause mid-line can convey shock, interruption, or a sudden violent event, forcing the reader to pause as the speaker might.

cards.front: What is the effect of contrasting imagery of home or peace within a conflict poem?
cards.back: It heightens the horror or loss of conflict by reminding the reader what has been destroyed or is unreachable, creating emotional contrast.

cards.front: Why might a poet choose a restrained, controlled tone to describe violence?
cards.back: Understatement can be more powerful than explicit horror, letting the facts or images speak for themselves and inviting the reader to supply the emotional response.

cards.front: What should you compare when two conflict poems share a similar theme, such as loss?
cards.back: Not just that both mention loss, but how each poet's structure, imagery, form and tone create a different presentation or attitude towards that loss.

cards.front: Give an example of a sound device used for violent effect in conflict poetry.
cards.back: Harsh plosive consonants (b, p, k, t) can mimic gunfire, explosions or physical blows, adding a visceral quality to the language.

cards.front: Why is identifying the poet's attitude to conflict part of a strong comparison?
cards.back: Poems on conflict can glorify, question, mourn or condemn war differently; naming that stance sharpens the comparison beyond just shared subject matter.

cloze: The Conflict cluster is one of {{c1::three}} themed clusters in the OCR Poetry Anthology.
A sudden pause within a line of poetry is called a {{c1::caesura}}, often used for shock in conflict poems.
Fragmented or disrupted {{c1::structure}} can be used to mirror the chaos of conflict.
Harsh {{c1::plosive}} consonants can be used to mimic violent sounds such as gunfire.

topics.name: OCR Poetry Anthology: Youth and Age Cluster
subtopics: This cluster is one of three options in the OCR Poetry Anthology 'Towards a World Unknown' - the family has not confirmed which cluster is studied, so treat this as preparation only until confirmed
The exam gives one named poem printed on the paper, plus a linked unseen poem; you compare the named poem with the unseen poem and may also be asked about a second anthology poem
Do not guess specific poem titles you are not certain belong to this cluster - focus revision on themes, comparative method and named poems only where certain

Likely thematic range for a Youth and Age cluster: childhood memory, the passage of time, generational relationships (parent/child, grandparent/grandchild), the loss of innocence, ageing and mortality, nostalgia for the past
Perspective in Youth and Age poetry: an adult narrator looking back at childhood, a child's voice, or an older figure reflecting on the young
Imagery patterns common in this theme: seasonal imagery to represent life stages, imagery of growth and decay, sensory or nostalgic imagery tied to specific memories
Structural devices: chronological structure tracing a life or memory, circular structure returning to a starting image, contrast between past and present tenses
Tone: nostalgic, wistful, regretful, celebratory, or a mix that shifts across the poem
Comparative method: identify a shared idea about time, memory or generational relationships, then compare how each poet's methods present it differently
Comparing form: a poem with a tight, regular form might suggest order or control over memory, while an irregular form may suggest memory's unreliability
Symbolism common to this theme: objects that outlast people (photographs, houses, clothes), physical signs of ageing, or thresholds like doorways marking change
Building flexible comparison points around tense, structure, imagery and tone so they can be adapted to whichever named poem appears
Practising with any unseen poem on memory, childhood or ageing to build confidence comparing methods under time pressure
Revision priority: since the studied poems are unconfirmed, prioritise comparative skills and terminology over memorising specific poem content

cards.front: What kinds of relationships or experiences might feature in a Youth and Age cluster?
cards.back: Childhood memory, generational relationships such as parent/child or grandparent/grandchild, the loss of innocence, ageing and mortality, and nostalgia for the past.

cards.front: Why might a poet use a shift between past and present tense in a poem about memory?
cards.back: It can show the gap between how something felt at the time and how it is remembered or understood now, highlighting change or loss.

cards.front: How can seasonal imagery be used to represent stages of life?
cards.back: Spring or summer can represent youth and growth, while autumn or winter can represent ageing, decline or approaching death.

cards.front: What might a circular (returning) structure suggest in a poem about memory?
cards.back: That the speaker is unable to move on from a particular moment, or that the memory continues to shape the present.

cards.front: Give an example of an object that might symbolise the passage of time in this cluster.
cards.back: A photograph, an old house or an item of clothing can outlast the people connected to it, symbolising memory, loss or the passing of time.

cards.front: How might tone shift across a poem about ageing or childhood?
cards.back: It might move from nostalgic warmth to regret, or from innocence to a more painful adult understanding, and identifying that shift is valuable for analysis.

cards.front: What should a comparison of two poems on this theme focus on beyond shared subject matter?
cards.back: How each poet's structure, imagery, tense and tone create a different attitude towards time, memory or the relationship being described.

cards.front: Why is an irregular poetic form sometimes suited to a poem about memory?
cards.back: It can suggest memory's unreliability or fragmented nature, contrasting with a tight, regular form that might suggest a controlled, ordered recollection.

cloze: The Youth and Age cluster is one of {{c1::three}} themed clusters in the OCR Poetry Anthology.
{{c1::Seasonal}} imagery, such as autumn or winter, can represent ageing or decline.
A {{c1::circular}} structure that returns to its starting image can suggest a speaker is unable to move on from a memory.
Objects such as {{c1::photographs}} can symbolise memory or the passing of time because they outlast people.

topics.name: Exam Skills and Essay Craft for J352
subtopics: Both components are closed text: no copies of the texts are allowed in the exam, so quotations must be memorised
AO1: informed personal response supported by textual references and quotations
AO2: analysis of language, form and structure using accurate subject terminology
AO3: understanding of the relationship between texts and their contexts (worth less overall than AO1/AO2)
AO4: accurate spelling, punctuation and range of vocabulary/sentence structures, assessed only in Section B of each component
Writing a conceptual thesis statement in the opening sentences that answers the question directly
Point-Method-Effect (or What-How-Why) paragraph structure: make a point, show the method with embedded evidence, explain the effect and link to the question
Embedding short, precise quotations inside your own sentence rather than dropping them in as a separate sentence
Zooming in on individual words within a quotation and offering more than one possible interpretation
Writing about form and structure explicitly, not only language choices, to access full AO2 marks
Weaving context into analysis as part of interpretation, not as a separate paragraph of historical facts
For extract-based questions (modern text has no extract, but 19th century prose and Shakespeare do): spend real time analysing the extract closely before ranging outward
Time management across a 2-hour paper with two 40-mark sections: roughly 45-50 minutes reading/planning/writing each section, leaving a few minutes to check
Planning in the first few minutes: identify the question's key words, choose a line of argument, and jot 3-4 topic sentences before writing
For the poetry comparison, planning both poems side by side before writing to identify shared and contrasting methods early
Final proofreading pass focused on sentence accuracy in Section B answers where AO4 is assessed

cards.front: Why must quotations be memorised for both OCR Literature components?
cards.back: Both components are closed text exams - no copies of the studied texts are permitted in the exam room.

cards.front: What is assessed by AO3 in OCR GCSE English Literature?
cards.back: Understanding of the relationship between texts and the contexts in which they were written, worth 15% of the whole qualification overall - less than AO1 or AO2.

cards.front: In which sections is AO4 assessed?
cards.back: Only in Section B of each component (19th century prose in Component 01, Shakespeare in Component 02), where it carries a separate small mark allocation for spelling, punctuation and sentence variety.

cards.front: What does the Point-Method-Effect paragraph structure mean?
cards.back: State the point you are making, show the method the writer uses with embedded evidence, then explain the effect on the reader or meaning and link back to the question.

cards.front: Why is embedding quotations better than dropping them into a separate sentence?
cards.back: It keeps the sentence fluent and lets you analyse individual words precisely within your own argument, which is exactly what AO2 rewards.

cards.front: How should you approach the extract in a 19th century prose or Shakespeare question?
cards.back: Analyse the extract closely first, since it is the anchor for the whole answer, before ranging outward to make links with the rest of the text.

cards.front: Roughly how much time should you spend on each 40-mark section in a 2-hour paper?
cards.back: Around 45-50 minutes each, leaving a short amount of time to check spelling, punctuation and grammar, especially in Section B answers.

cards.front: What should you do in the first few minutes before writing an essay?
cards.back: Identify the key words in the question, decide your line of argument (thesis), and jot 3-4 topic sentences to structure your paragraphs.

cards.front: Why weave context into analysis rather than writing a separate context paragraph?
cards.back: AO3 rewards context that shapes interpretation of the text, not standalone historical facts disconnected from the question.

cards.front: Give one useful technique for offering deeper analysis of a quotation.
cards.back: Zoom in on a single word within the quotation and offer more than one plausible interpretation of its effect or connotation.

cloze: Both OCR Literature components are {{c1::closed text}}, so all quotations must be {{c2::memorised}}.
AO4 is only assessed in {{c1::Section B}} of each component.
The paragraph structure Point-{{c1::Method}}-{{c2::Effect}} keeps analysis focused on the writer's technique and its impact.
AO3 (context) carries a {{c1::smaller}} overall weighting than AO1 or AO2 in this specification.
A strong essay opens with a {{c1::thesis}} statement that directly answers the question.

exams.name: Component 01: Exploring modern and literary heritage texts

examNote: Dates are from the OCR final examination timetable for June 2027: Component 01 Wednesday 12 May 2027 am and Component 02 Wednesday 19 May 2027 am, each 2 hours.

commandWords.means: Investigate a character, theme or moment in depth, considering multiple angles and possible interpretations.
commandWords.doThis: Do not just describe what happens - offer an interpretation, support it with embedded quotations, and consider alternative readings.

commandWords.means: Examine two texts or poems together, looking at similarities and differences in ideas and methods.
commandWords.doThis: Write about both poems in every paragraph rather than one after the other, using linking words like 'similarly' or 'whereas'.

commandWords.means: Asks you to identify a writer's methods and their effects on the reader or the meaning of the text.
commandWords.doThis: Name the technique or method, quote it, then explain the effect it creates and why the writer chose it.

commandWords.means: An evaluative question giving a statement or view that you must judge, using evidence from the text.
commandWords.doThis: Decide your overall position early, then build a case using evidence from at least two moments in the text, acknowledging any complexity.

commandWords.means: Asks how a writer shows or constructs an idea, character or theme through their choices as a writer.
commandWords.doThis: Focus on the writer's deliberate choices (language, structure, form) rather than retelling the plot.

commandWords.means: Break language, form or structure down into its parts and examine how each part creates meaning or effect.
commandWords.doThis: Zoom in on individual words or techniques, and explain precisely how they work rather than giving a general impression.

commandWords.means: Weigh up an idea from more than one angle before reaching a view.
commandWords.doThis: Present at least two ways of reading the moment or theme, then show which reading you find most convincing and why.

commandWords.means: You must move beyond the printed extract to discuss other moments across the whole text.
commandWords.doThis: Choose two or three additional moments that develop or complicate the idea shown in the extract, not just similar repeats of it.

commandWords.means: The impact a writer's choice has on the reader's understanding, feelings or interpretation.
commandWords.doThis: Always follow up 'what' a writer does with 'so what' - state precisely what impression or feeling is created and why.

sections.title: Quotation bank: Macbeth
sections.note: Learn these exactly, including which character speaks them, so they can be embedded accurately in a closed-book exam.

items.term: So foul and fair a day I have not seen
items.detail: Macbeth, Act 1 Scene 3. Echoes the witches' 'fair is foul, foul is fair' and shows Macbeth already speaking in their paradoxical language, hinting at his susceptibility to their influence.

items.term: Stars, hide your fires; let not light see my black and deep desires
items.detail: Macbeth, Act 1 Scene 4. Shows Macbeth consciously choosing to hide his murderous ambition, proving he understands his own moral corruption from early in the play.

items.term: Look like the innocent flower, but be the serpent under't
items.detail: Lady Macbeth to Macbeth, Act 1 Scene 5. Establishes the deception/appearance-versus-reality theme and Lady Macbeth's ruthless practicality compared to Macbeth's hesitancy.

items.term: Screw your courage to the sticking-place
items.detail: Lady Macbeth, Act 1 Scene 7. Shows her manipulating Macbeth's sense of masculinity and courage to push him towards regicide.

items.term: Is this a dagger which I see before me
items.detail: Macbeth, Act 2 Scene 1. Opens the famous soliloquy showing his guilt-ridden hallucination before Duncan's murder, revealing his conscience is already at war with his ambition.

items.term: Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood clean from my hand?
items.detail: Macbeth, Act 2 Scene 2. Shows immediate, overwhelming guilt after killing Duncan; blood becomes a symbol of guilt that cannot be washed away.

items.term: A little water clears us of this deed
items.detail: Lady Macbeth, Act 2 Scene 2. Contrasts her apparent coldness and practicality with Macbeth's horror, though this composure later collapses into guilt in Act 5.

items.term: Duncan is in his grave; after life's fitful fever he sleeps well
items.detail: Macbeth, Act 3 Scene 2. Shows Macbeth's growing envy of the dead and his own tormented, sleepless guilt as king.

items.term: It will have blood; they say, blood will have blood
items.detail: Macbeth, Act 3 Scene 4, after seeing Banquo's ghost. Shows his belief that murder demands retribution, foreshadowing his own downfall.

items.term: By the pricking of my thumbs, something wicked this way comes
items.detail: Second Witch, Act 4 Scene 1. Shows how far Macbeth has fallen - even the witches now identify him as the embodiment of evil approaching.

items.term: Double, double toil and trouble; fire burn and cauldron bubble
items.detail: Witches, Act 4 Scene 1. Reinforces the supernatural, ritualistic atmosphere surrounding the prophecies that further seal Macbeth's fate.

items.term: Out, damned spot! Out, I say!
items.detail: Lady Macbeth, Act 5 Scene 1 (sleepwalking scene). Shows her mental collapse and inability to escape guilt she could not voice while awake.

items.term: Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player that struts and frets his hour upon the stage
items.detail: Macbeth, Act 5 Scene 5, on hearing of Lady Macbeth's death. Shows his descent into nihilism and despair, believing life to be meaningless.

items.term: Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow
items.detail: Macbeth, Act 5 Scene 5. Opens the famous despairing soliloquy on the meaningless repetition of time, reflecting his total loss of hope and purpose.

items.term: I bear a charmed life, which must not yield to one of woman born
items.detail: Macbeth, Act 5 Scene 8. Shows his false confidence in the witches' prophecy just before Macduff reveals he was not 'of woman born' in the natural sense, leading to Macbeth's defeat.

items.term: Lay on, Macduff, and damned be him that first cries 'Hold, enough!'
items.detail: Macbeth, Act 5 Scene 8, his final line. Shows he dies fighting rather than surrendering, a final flash of the soldierly courage seen in Act 1.

items.term: This dead butcher and his fiend-like queen
items.detail: Malcolm, Act 5 Scene 9. The play's final judgement on the Macbeths, showing how far they have fallen from the noble figures introduced at the start.

items.term: Brave Macbeth (well he deserves that name)
items.detail: The Sergeant/Captain, Act 1 Scene 2. Establishes Macbeth's initial heroism and reputation before his moral decline, useful for tracking his full character arc.

items.term: When shall we three meet again?
items.detail: First Witch, Act 1 Scene 1. Opens the play, immediately establishing a supernatural, ominous atmosphere before any human character appears.

items.term: Nought's had, all's spent, where our desire is got without content
items.detail: Lady Macbeth, Act 3 Scene 2. Shows that achieving the throne has brought no satisfaction, reinforcing the theme that unchecked ambition is ultimately self-destructive.

sections.title: Quotation bank: The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
sections.note: Chapter references follow the standard ten-chapter structure. Learn who narrates each quotation - Utterson's narrative, Lanyon's letter, or Jekyll's final statement.

items.term: There is something wrong with his appearance; something displeasing, something downright detestable
items.detail: Enfield describing Hyde, Chapter 1. Establishes the instinctive revulsion Hyde provokes despite no one being able to define exactly why - hints at an unnatural, primitive quality.

items.term: O my poor old Harry Jekyll, if ever I read Satan's signature upon a face, it is on that of your new friend
items.detail: Utterson, Chapter 2. Religious imagery marks Hyde as evil, and shows even the rational lawyer resorting to the supernatural to explain him - a key Gothic move. Note the affectionate 'Harry', which sets up Utterson's loyalty as a motive for the whole investigation.

items.term: If he be Mr Hyde, I shall be Mr Seek
items.detail: Utterson, Chapter 2. Shows the lawyer's rational, investigative determination and sets up the novel's detective/mystery structure.

items.term: Man is not truly one, but truly two
items.detail: Jekyll's final statement, Chapter 10. States the novel's central theme of duality directly - every person contains both a civilised and a primitive self.

items.term: All human beings...are commingled out of good and evil
items.detail: Jekyll's final statement, Chapter 10. Extends the duality theme to all humanity, not just Jekyll, universalising the novel's moral warning.

items.term: He had a kind of black sneering coolness...like Satan
items.detail: Enfield, Chapter 1, describing Hyde after the trampling of the girl. Religious imagery aligns Hyde explicitly with Satan and evil; Enfield stresses Hyde's calm, which is more frightening than rage. Use for: Hyde as pure evil, Gothic villain, first impressions.

items.term: I saw that ... I was slowly losing hold of my original and better self
items.detail: Jekyll's final statement, Chapter 10. Shows Jekyll's growing loss of control over the transformations, addiction to being Hyde, and his own moral collapse.

items.term: Hyde grew in stature...as if he were slowly liquefying
items.detail: Jekyll's final statement, Chapter 10. Physically enacts the growing dominance of Hyde over Jekyll, symbolising evil overtaking the civilised self.

items.term: The most racking pangs succeeded: a grinding in the bones, deadly nausea
items.detail: Jekyll's final statement, describing the transformation, Chapter 10. Shows the transformation is physically violent and painful, reinforcing that unleashing one's darker nature has a real cost.

items.term: This, too, was myself
items.detail: Jekyll's final statement, Chapter 10. Jekyll's admission that Hyde is not a separate being but genuinely part of him, reinforcing that evil is innate rather than external.

items.term: London has nothing like him
items.detail: Enfield describing Hyde's unsettling presence, Chapter 1. Shows Hyde as uniquely disturbing even in a large, morally complex Victorian city.

items.term: He was perfectly cool and made no resistance, but gave me one look so ugly
items.detail: Description of Hyde after trampling the girl, Chapter 1. Shows Hyde's total lack of remorse and casual cruelty, foreshadowing the later murder of Carew.

items.term: It wasn't like a man; it was like some damned Juggernaut
items.detail: Enfield's account of Hyde trampling the girl, Chapter 1. Dehumanises Hyde from the earliest description, foreshadowing his non-human, primitive nature.

items.term: The doctor was confounded... he grew pale, and a shudder overtook him
items.detail: Reaction of the doctor treating the trampled girl on seeing Hyde, Chapter 1. Shows even a professional, rational man reacts instinctively with horror to Hyde's presence.

items.term: With a transient sense of unfamiliarity...a leap of welcome
items.detail: Jekyll's final statement describing his first transformation, Chapter 10. Shows Jekyll's initial excitement and freedom in becoming Hyde, before the addiction turns destructive.

items.term: I felt younger, lighter, happier in body
items.detail: Jekyll's final statement, Chapter 10. Shows the seductive appeal of shedding respectable restraint, explaining why Jekyll continues the experiment despite the danger.

items.term: Since I had learned to dread the direction of my worse self, I would...forget in the pursuit of pleasure
items.detail: Jekyll's final statement, Chapter 10. Reveals Jekyll's underlying hedonism and desire to escape the moral restrictions of Victorian respectability.

items.term: He is now become the beast that was within me
items.detail: Jekyll's final statement, Chapter 10. Confirms that Hyde represents an internal, innate evil rather than something externally created, reinforcing the duality theme.

items.term: The pleasures which I made haste to seek in my disguise were...undignified
items.detail: Jekyll's final statement, Chapter 10. Hints, without full disclosure (a Victorian narrative convention), at Hyde's vices, letting the reader infer moral transgression.

items.term: Utterson stood a while when Mr Hyde had left him, the picture of disquietude
items.detail: Chapter 2, after Utterson's first meeting with Hyde. Shows Utterson's rational unease, reinforcing that Hyde provokes instinctive fear even in level-headed characters.

sections.title: Quotation bank: An Inspector Calls
sections.note: This is a play with no printed extract in the exam, so precise, correctly-attributed quotations are essential for the whole-text essay.

items.term: The Titanic...unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable
items.detail: Mr Birling, Act 1. Dramatic irony undermines his authority and capitalist confidence immediately, since the audience knows the Titanic sank.

items.term: A man has to make his own way...has to look after himself and his own
items.detail: Mr Birling, Act 1. States the capitalist, individualist philosophy that the play systematically dismantles through the Inspector's investigation.

items.term: The way some of these cranks talk and write now, you'd think everybody has to look after everybody else
items.detail: Mr Birling, Act 1. Dismisses socialist ideas, which Priestley uses to make Birling appear foolish and out of touch to a post-war audience.

items.term: I don't think you ought to have said that to her about her not being one of the family
items.detail: Sheila to Gerald, Act 3. Marks the start of her ability to judge her own family and fiance critically, showing her moral development.

items.term: We are members of one body. We all have to share something
items.detail: The Inspector, Act 1. States Priestley's central socialist message of collective responsibility directly to the audience.

items.term: But these girls aren't cheap labour - they're people
items.detail: Sheila, Act 1. Shows Sheila's growing moral awareness and empathy, contrasting with her parents' view of workers as mere resources.

items.term: I'll never, never do it again to anybody
items.detail: Sheila, Act 1, after learning of her role in Eva's dismissal. Shows genuine remorse and change, distinct from her parents' denial.

items.term: The girl killed herself - and died a horrible death. But each of you helped to kill her
items.detail: The Inspector, Act 3. Directly states the play's central argument that individual actions have collective consequences.

items.term: If you don't come down sharply on some of these people, they'd soon be asking for the earth
items.detail: Mr Birling, Act 1, on why he refused Eva's pay rise request. Reveals his ruthless, self-interested attitude to his workers.

items.term: I was in a state when a girl says she'll do anything to help
items.detail: Eric, Act 3, admitting his exploitation of Eva. Shows his guilt and immaturity, contrasting with his parents' refusal to accept blame.

items.term: You're the one I blame for this
items.detail: Sheila to Gerald, Act 2, on learning of his affair with Eva/Daisy. Shows Sheila's honesty and refusal to pretend all is well, unlike the older generation.

items.term: Fire and blood and anguish
items.detail: The Inspector's final speech, Act 3. Warns of war and suffering if society does not learn collective responsibility - dramatic irony for a 1945 audience who had lived through two world wars.

items.term: The famous younger generation who know it all. And they can't even take a joke
items.detail: Mrs Birling, Act 3. Shows her dismissive, condescending attitude to Sheila and Eric's growing conscience, reinforcing her refusal to change.

items.term: I did nothing I'm ashamed of
items.detail: Mrs Birling, Act 2, defending her refusal to help Eva through the charity committee. Shows her total lack of self-awareness and hypocrisy.

items.term: She was giving herself ridiculous airs
items.detail: Mrs Birling on Eva Smith, Act 2. Reveals Mrs Birling's class snobbery, judging Eva for daring to use the name 'Mrs Birling'.

items.term: Just used the phrase I'd been thinking myself
items.detail: Gerald, Act 3, on the Inspector possibly repeating others' words. Shows Gerald's relief in seeking ways to discredit the Inspector rather than face guilt.

items.term: Everything's all right now, Sheila. What about this ring?
items.detail: Gerald, Act 3, once he believes the Inspector was a hoax. Shows he wants to return to the status quo rather than learn anything, unlike Sheila.

items.term: Public men, Mr Birling, have responsibilities as well as privileges
items.detail: The Inspector, Act 1. Directly challenges Birling's belief that status brings only rights and no duties, reinforcing the responsibility theme.

items.term: It's the way I like to be treated by a maid
items.detail: Mr Birling, Act 1, on Eva's dismissal from Milward's over a customer complaint. Shows his casual complicity in class-based cruelty even when not the direct cause.

items.term: One Eva Smith has gone - but there are millions and millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths still left with us
items.detail: The Inspector, Act 3. Universalises Eva's story, extending the moral warning beyond this one family to society as a whole.

sections.title: Assessment objectives in plain English and how marks split
sections.note: Percentages are of the whole GCSE. AO4 (SPaG) is assessed only in Section B of each component.

items.term: AO1
items.detail: Read, understand and respond to texts: give an informed personal response and support it with textual references and quotations. Worth 40% of the whole GCSE overall - the single biggest AO.

items.term: AO2
items.detail: Analyse the language, form and structure a writer uses to create meanings and effects, using accurate subject terminology. Also worth 40% overall, jointly the biggest AO with AO1.

items.term: AO3
items.detail: Show understanding of the relationship between texts and the contexts in which they were written. Worth only 15% overall - do not let context dominate an answer at the expense of AO1/AO2.

items.term: AO4
items.detail: Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation. Worth 5% overall, assessed only in Section B of each component (19th century prose and Shakespeare).

items.term: Component 01 AO split
items.detail: Exploring modern and literary heritage texts is worth 50% of the GCSE overall: within it, AO1 carries about 20%, AO2 about 17.5%, AO3 about 10%, AO4 about 2.5% (Section B only).

items.term: Component 02 AO split
items.detail: Exploring poetry and Shakespeare is worth 50% of the GCSE overall: within it, AO1 carries about 20%, AO2 about 22.5%, AO3 about 5%, AO4 about 2.5% (Shakespeare, Section B only).

items.term: Why AO1 and AO2 dominate
items.detail: Together they make up 80% of the whole qualification, so every paragraph should combine a clear personal response (AO1) with close analysis of the writer's methods (AO2).

items.term: Comparison across the qualification
items.detail: 25% of all marks in the specification relate to tasks requiring comparison between texts - this includes the modern text extract comparison and the poetry comparison.

items.term: Where AO3 earns marks
items.detail: AO3 rewards context that is used to deepen interpretation of a specific moment or choice in the text, not standalone historical facts stated without being linked to meaning.

items.term: AO4 marking in Section B
items.detail: AO4 uses a separate short marking grid assessing accuracy of spelling and punctuation and range of vocabulary and sentence structures, worth a small number of extra marks on top of the main AO1-3 marks.

sections.title: Essay structure and timing for each section
sections.note: Each component is 2 hours for 80 marks across two 40-mark sections - budget roughly half the time to each, leaving a few minutes to check.

items.term: Component 01 Section A: Modern prose or drama (no extract)
items.detail: No extract is printed. Choose one of two whole-text essay questions. Spend 5 minutes planning a thesis and 3-4 topic sentences, then write 4-5 Point-Method-Effect paragraphs across about 40 minutes, leaving a couple of minutes to check.

items.term: Component 01 Section B: 19th century prose (extract given)
items.detail: An extract is printed; the question asks you to discuss it and then range 'elsewhere in the novel'. Spend 5-8 minutes annotating the extract closely, then write roughly half your answer on the extract and half ranging outward, in about 40 minutes total including AO4 accuracy.

items.term: Component 02 Section A: Poetry across time (named plus unseen poem)
items.detail: A named anthology poem and a linked unseen poem are printed. Spend 5-8 minutes annotating both for shared and contrasting methods, then write in an integrated, poem-by-poem-in-every-paragraph structure across about 40 minutes.

items.term: Component 02 Section B: Shakespeare (extract given)
items.detail: An extract is printed; the question asks you to discuss it and then range across the whole play. Spend 5-8 minutes annotating the extract, write roughly half on the extract and half elsewhere in the play, across about 40 minutes, saving time to check AO4 accuracy.

items.term: Opening thesis sentence
items.detail: State a clear, conceptual argument that directly answers the question in your first one or two sentences, e.g. 'Priestley presents Sheila as the character most capable of moral growth, using her arc to model the collective responsibility he wants his audience to adopt.'

items.term: Point-Method-Effect paragraph shape
items.detail: Point: state the idea. Method: embed a short quotation showing the technique. Effect: explain precisely what impression or meaning this creates and link it back to the question.

items.term: How much time to spend on the extract versus 'elsewhere'
items.detail: For extract-based questions, aim for roughly equal time and space on the printed extract and on the rest of the text - staying only in the extract caps marks in the middle bands.

items.term: Concluding a literature essay
items.detail: Do not simply summarise; end by returning to the conceptual thesis and stating what the overall analysis reveals about the writer's wider purpose or message.

items.term: Timing checkpoint
items.detail: If a component is 2 hours for 80 marks, you should be starting your second section by the 60-minute mark; if you are still writing your first answer past that point, move on and return only if time allows.

items.term: Final minutes
items.detail: Use any remaining minutes to check that quotations are accurately remembered and that Section B answers (19th century prose, Shakespeare) have accurate spelling, punctuation and varied sentence structures for AO4.

items.term: Soliloquy
items.detail: A speech delivered by a character alone on stage, revealing inner thoughts the audience can trust as sincere - high-value evidence for character analysis.

items.term: Dramatic irony
items.detail: When the audience knows something a character does not, creating tension, foreboding or moral judgement of that character.

items.term: Foreshadowing
items.detail: An early hint or clue about events that will happen later in the text, building tension or preparing the reader/audience.

items.term: Stagecraft
items.detail: The practical elements of staging a play - lighting, set, props, entrances and exits - used deliberately by a playwright to create meaning.

items.term: Duality
items.detail: The idea that a person or thing contains two opposing natures or identities, central to Jekyll and Hyde and relevant to conflicted characters generally.

items.term: Gothic convention
items.detail: A recurring feature of Gothic fiction: the uncanny, oppressive settings, decay, transgression of natural limits, and the blurring of good and evil.

items.term: Frame narrative
items.detail: A story told inside another story or through embedded documents (letters, testimonies), distancing the reader and often raising questions of reliability.

items.term: Motif
items.detail: An image, idea or phrase that recurs throughout a text, building cumulative meaning, e.g. blood in Macbeth or doors in Jekyll and Hyde.

items.term: Pathetic fallacy
items.detail: Giving the natural world human emotions or using weather/nature to reflect a character's mood or a play's atmosphere, e.g. the storm after Duncan's murder.

items.term: Volta
items.detail: A turn or shift in argument, tone or mood within a poem, classically found around line 9 of a Petrarchan sonnet.

items.term: Enjambment
items.detail: A sentence or phrase that runs over a line break without punctuation, creating flow, urgency or surprise.

items.term: Caesura
items.detail: A deliberate pause within a line of poetry, usually created by punctuation, often used for emphasis or sudden shock.

items.term: Dramatic monologue
items.detail: A poem spoken in the voice of a single created character, often revealing something about them that they do not intend to reveal.

items.term: Extended metaphor
items.detail: A metaphor developed and sustained across multiple lines or an entire poem, deepening a single comparison.

items.term: Juxtaposition
items.detail: Placing two contrasting ideas, images or characters close together to highlight their difference.

items.term: Symbolism
items.detail: Using an object, person or place to represent a wider idea beyond its literal meaning, e.g. Banquo's ghost symbolising Macbeth's guilt.

items.term: Tragic hero
items.detail: A protagonist, often of noble status, whose own flaw (hamartia) leads to their downfall, as with Macbeth's ambition.

items.term: Foil
items.detail: A character whose qualities contrast with another character, highlighting the second character's traits by comparison, e.g. Banquo as a foil to Macbeth.

items.term: Anaphora
items.detail: The deliberate repetition of a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses or lines for emphasis, e.g. 'tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow'.

items.term: Allegory
items.detail: A narrative in which characters and events stand for wider political, moral or historical ideas beyond the literal story.

items.term: Macbeth: King James I and the divine right of kings
items.detail: James I believed monarchs were appointed by God (divine right), so a play in which killing a king unleashes chaos and disorder would have resonated as morally and politically correct to him.

items.term: Macbeth: the Gunpowder Plot (1605)
items.detail: Shakespeare wrote Macbeth shortly after an assassination attempt on James I was foiled, making a play about the horror and consequences of regicide especially topical.

items.term: Macbeth: Jacobean beliefs about witchcraft
items.detail: James I had written a book on witchcraft (Daemonologie) and witch trials were common; a Jacobean audience would have taken the witches' supernatural power seriously, not as fantasy.

items.term: Macbeth: the Great Chain of Being
items.detail: A Jacobean belief that the universe had a fixed hierarchical order (God, king, nobles, commoners, nature); regicide was seen as a crime against this cosmic order, explaining the unnatural disorder after Duncan's murder.

items.term: Jekyll and Hyde: Victorian respectability
items.detail: Victorian society placed huge importance on public reputation; men in particular were expected to maintain a respectable public image regardless of private conduct, explaining Jekyll's need for a hidden outlet.

items.term: Jekyll and Hyde: Darwin and evolutionary anxiety
items.detail: Charles Darwin's theory of evolution (1859) raised fears that humans were closer to animals than previously believed; Hyde's ape-like, primitive appearance reflects this anxiety about a hidden 'animal' nature in man.

items.term: Jekyll and Hyde: the Gothic double/doppelganger tradition
items.detail: Stevenson was writing within a tradition of 'double' narratives exploring a hidden or evil twin self, tapping into contemporary fascination with psychology and the unconscious mind.

items.term: Jekyll and Hyde: real Victorian double lives
items.detail: Late-Victorian London had well-publicised cases of respectable public figures living secret, scandalous double lives, which likely informed the novel's exploration of hidden vice behind a genteel facade.

items.term: An Inspector Calls: the 1912 setting
items.detail: Set shortly before the sinking of the Titanic (1912) and the First World War (1914-18), a period of confident, complacent optimism among the wealthy that Priestley uses ironically.

items.term: An Inspector Calls: written and first performed in 1945
items.detail: Priestley wrote the play as the Second World War ended, hoping Britain would build a fairer, more socialist post-war society rather than return to pre-war inequality.

items.term: An Inspector Calls: Priestley's socialism
items.detail: Priestley was a committed socialist who believed in collective responsibility and a fairer distribution of wealth, views he expresses directly through the Inspector's speeches.

items.term: An Inspector Calls: the birth of the welfare state
items.detail: The play anticipates ideas that shaped the UK's post-war welfare state (founded 1945-48), reflecting a shift towards state responsibility for citizens' wellbeing.

items.term: An Inspector Calls: Edwardian class and gender attitudes
items.detail: In 1912, working-class women like Eva Smith had very limited legal or economic protection and were dependent on the goodwill of employers, explaining her vulnerability to the Birlings and Gerald.

items.term: General: the 19th century Poor Law and workhouses
items.detail: The Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834 sent destitute people into workhouses with harsh conditions, reflecting Victorian attitudes that poverty was often a moral failing rather than a social problem - relevant background for any 19th century prose text.

items.term: General: comparison weighting
items.detail: 25% of all marks across the whole GCSE English Literature specification relate to tasks that require comparison, underlining why comparative skills matter beyond just the poetry section.

items.term: Opening a comparative thesis
items.detail: Both [poem/text A] and [poem/text B] explore the idea of ___, but while [A] presents it as ___, [B] instead suggests ___.

items.term: Introducing a shared method
items.detail: Both poets use ___ to convey ___, though the effect differs because ___.

items.term: Introducing a contrasting method
items.detail: Whereas [poet A] relies on ___ to suggest ___, [poet B] instead uses ___ to create a sense of ___.

items.term: Linking two poems in one sentence
items.detail: This mirrors/contrasts with the way [poem B] presents a similar/different idea through ___.

items.term: Discourse markers for comparison
items.detail: Similarly; in contrast; whereas; by contrast; in a comparable way; conversely; on the other hand; just as ___, so too ___.

items.term: Evaluating 'how far do you agree'
items.detail: To a significant extent, [text] supports this view, since ___; however, this reading is complicated by ___.

items.term: Introducing a qualification
items.detail: While this is true in [moment], the picture becomes more complex when ___.

items.term: Making a tentative interpretation
items.detail: This could suggest ___, or perhaps more convincingly, it implies ___.

items.term: Concluding an evaluative paragraph
items.detail: Ultimately, this suggests that [writer] wants the reader/audience to ___.

items.term: Linking context to interpretation
items.detail: This reflects the [Victorian/Jacobean/post-war] belief that ___, which deepens our understanding of ___.

items.term: Analysing effect precisely
items.detail: This choice of ___ creates an impression of ___, forcing the reader/audience to ___.

items.term: Comparing writer's overall purpose
items.detail: Both writers seem to want their audience to reconsider ___, but [A] achieves this through ___ while [B] achieves it through ___.

items.term: Component 01 (J352/01): Exploring modern and literary heritage texts
items.detail: 2 hours, 80 marks, closed text. Section A: modern prose or drama essay, no extract, choice of two questions, about 40 minutes. Section B: 19th century prose extract question plus 'elsewhere in the novel', about 40 minutes including AO4 accuracy. Spend 5 minutes planning each section; leave 2-3 minutes at the end to check quotations and spelling.

items.term: Component 01 Section A time split
items.detail: Of the roughly 40 minutes: 5 minutes reading the question and planning a thesis with 3-4 topic sentences, 32-33 minutes writing 4-5 Point-Method-Effect paragraphs on An Inspector Calls, 2 minutes checking quotation accuracy.

items.term: Component 01 Section B time split
items.detail: Of the roughly 40 minutes: 5-8 minutes annotating the printed Jekyll and Hyde extract, then split the remaining time evenly between close analysis of the extract and moving 'elsewhere in the novel', with 2-3 minutes left for AO4 accuracy checks.

items.term: Component 02 (J352/02): Exploring poetry and Shakespeare
items.detail: 2 hours, 80 marks, closed text. Section A: named anthology poem plus a linked unseen poem for comparison, about 40 minutes, spend 5-8 minutes annotating both poems before writing. Section B: Shakespeare extract plus 'elsewhere in the play', about 40 minutes including AO4 accuracy. Leave 2-3 minutes at the end to check quotations and spelling.

items.term: Component 02 Section A time split
items.detail: Of the roughly 40 minutes: 5-8 minutes annotating the named poem and unseen poem for shared and contrasting methods, 30 minutes writing an integrated comparison (both poems in every paragraph), 2 minutes for a final check.

items.term: Component 02 Section B time split
items.detail: Of the roughly 40 minutes: 5-8 minutes annotating the printed Macbeth extract, then split the remaining time evenly between the extract and moving 'elsewhere in the play', with 2-3 minutes left for AO4 accuracy checks since this is the other section where AO4 is marked.

items.term: The night before both papers
items.detail: Re-read your quotation banks for all three set texts once rather than trying to learn new material; sleep matters more than last-minute cramming for a closed-book exam.

items.term: On the morning of each paper
items.detail: Quickly recite 3-4 key quotations per text from memory to warm up recall; check you have pens, a spare pen, and your exam equipment list.

items.term: If a question looks unfamiliar
items.detail: Break it into key words, decide which theme or character it is really asking about, and use your flexible quotation bank rather than panicking about a 'new' angle.

items.term: Halfway checkpoint in each paper
items.detail: By the 60-minute mark in a 2-hour paper you should be starting your second section; if Section A has overrun significantly, move to Section B and return only if time remains at the end.
